{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# The server was part of the appliance

A connected-home vendor has announced that it is closing the cloud service (the remote computers and software that keep its devices connected). The shutdown may be described as the retirement of an online feature, but that description misses the central defect. The server was part of the appliance—even if it sat in a distant data center instead of inside the plastic case.

When that server disappears, the hardware may still look perfectly healthy. Lights can light, motors can turn, sensors can sense. Yet the app (the phone software used to control the device) may stop signing in. Remote access may vanish. Automations (timed or event-triggered actions) may no longer run. Voice integrations (connections to another company’s assistant) may fail. Alerts might never arrive, and settings that were stored remotely might become impossible to change. A working appliance can become a collection of stranded parts.

A vendor may have legitimate reasons to end a service. Operating infrastructure costs money, old systems can be difficult to secure, and a shrinking customer base can make continued support impractical. Those concerns are real—but they don’t answer the question owners face. What exactly did the company sell?

Imagine that you bought a switch advertised as controllable from a phone. The box, product page, and setup process treated that control as an ordinary feature. If the vendor later disables it, the loss isn’t comparable to ending an optional newsletter. The company has removed part of the product’s practical function. The bargain included hardware, software, and continuing access to the system that joined them together.

Fine print doesn’t magically change that structure. A disclaimer may reserve broad power to alter a service, but the existence of a clause does not make a central feature incidental. Nor does ownership become meaningless merely because software participates in the device. Users paid for an appliance that performed certain tasks—not for a shell whose useful life could be ended by a server decision. The shutdown changes the original bargain because one party can withdraw performance after the other has already paid.

Local operation offers a straightforward protection. A device that can accept commands over the local network (LAN) can keep doing its basic job without contacting the vendor. Schedules can live on the device or on a controller in the home. Authentication (proof that a command is authorized) can happen locally. Essential settings can remain available through a documented interface, and owners can move their automations to another controller instead of rebuilding the household around a replacement product.

Local control won’t preserve every feature. Remote access still needs some route into the home, outside integrations may depend on other companies, and security updates require an ongoing maintenance plan. But basic operation should not collapse merely because one company stops paying a hosting bill. A thermostat should still regulate temperature. A switch should still switch. A lock should not lose ordinary management functions because an account server has gone dark.

The distinction also changes incentives. If cloud access is the only path to the appliance, the vendor holds a permanent veto over its operation—a kill switch built into the business model. If core functions work locally, closing the cloud service becomes a reduction in convenience rather than the destruction of the product. That gives companies room to leave a market without forcing every owner to leave with them.

We believe vendors should disclose, before sale, which functions depend on remote infrastructure, what happens when that infrastructure closes, and whether owners can operate the device locally. They should also provide a usable export format (a documented way to retrieve settings and records), a reasonable support period (a stated minimum rather than an aspiration), and a shutdown plan that preserves core functions wherever technically possible. Promises alone will not protect owners.

Regulators and lawmakers should treat remote services that are necessary for advertised functions as part of the product, not as disposable decoration. They should not permit companies to market durable appliances while reserving the practical power to erase them. We therefore urge vendors to build for local operation and regulators to require clear support and shutdown terms at the point of sale. If the server is part of the appliance, the law and the product design must finally recognize it.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
